articleSummary: Sporothrix brasiliensis, a fungal pathogen in the Sporothrix genus, is the most aggressive cause of sporotrichosis and shows efficient mammal-to-mammal transmission, especially among cats. Originating in Brazil in the 1990s, it now affects multiple South American countries; Brazil accounts for the majority of cases, with over 11,000 human infections reported in the last decade, per WHO. Cats develop ulcers, cutaneous nodules, lymphadenopathy, and facial/paw lesions; stray cats facilitate wide environmental dissemination through bites, scratches, and contact with contaminated secretions. Humans acquire infection mainly via scratches, bites, or contact with lesion secretions; initial lesion appears 1–12 weeks after exposure, then sporotrichoid lymphatic spread. Skin and subcutaneous tissue are most affected, but joints, lungs, and CNS can be involved. Immunocompromised individuals may develop severe disease, including meningitis or pneumonia. At ASM Microbe, CDC’s Shawn Lockhart warned introduction to the United States is imminent, signaling regional spread to Chile, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Argentina.

articleSummary: As of 27 June 2026, diphtheria is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae and targets the upper respiratory tract, with toxin potentially damaging the heart, kidneys, and brain if untreated. Transmission is mainly via respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing, and by contact with contaminated objects. The hallmark early sign is a grayish membrane on the throat and tonsils; other symptoms include sore throat, hoarseness, cough, runny nose, fever, weakness, and swollen neck lymph nodes. Symptoms typically appear 2–5 days after exposure, though some infections are asymptomatic yet contagious. High-risk groups include the unvaccinated, crowded areas with poor sanitation, travelers to outbreak regions, and the immunocompromised. Severe cases require emergency care for breathing difficulties or pale/blue skin. Prevention relies on the DPT vaccine (diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus); Indonesia uses this vaccine with hygiene measures.

articleSummary: Dong Thap province in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta contained an H5N1 avian influenza outbreak in Tan Thoi commune (Tan Hoa village) with no human infections reported. A total of 405 birds were culled—190 75-day-old Muscovy ducks, 210 13-day-old Muscovy ducks, three chickens and two geese; the flock was unvaccinated and not eligible for compensation. Disinfection, quarantine, and safe disposal were implemented, and 500 litres of disinfectant distributed. articleSummary: On 2026-06-27, a 62-year-old woman in Fujian was diagnosed with hepatic alveolar echinococcosis (liver parasitic lesion), with the largest lesion measuring 8.6 cm. Li Haitao, head physician at Fujian Medical University’s Mengchao Hepatobiliary Hospital, explains that the disease results from infection with eggs of the dog tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis. Its aggressive invasion and high recurrence earn it the nickname 'alveolar echinococcosis' or 'worm cancer' and it is a zoonosis mainly circulating in China’s northwest pastoral regions. Infection occurs when eggs on the fur of dogs contaminate food or water; after ingestion, larvae penetrate the intestinal wall and lodge in the liver, gradually invading tissue and potentially spreading to lungs or brain via lymphatic or blood routes. For dog owners, routine deworming, avoiding feeding dogs offal, limiting contact with stray dogs, and avoiding untreated water or contact with livestock and wildlife in pastoral areas are advised.

articleSummary: Monsoon humidity and stagnant water boost Aedes mosquito breeding, causing dengue and chikungunya cases to rise from July to October. There is no specific cure; prevention hinges on avoiding bites and eliminating breeding sites around the home—empty or dry containers, broken pots, coolers, tires, and other gathered water should be cleaned or dried weekly. Dress in light-colored, loose clothing that covers arms and legs; use repellents (creams, sprays, roll-ons) and install nets on doors/windows; sleep under a mosquito net. Community actions like fogging are advised if waterlogging occurs. Maintain cleanliness by preventing standing water, covering tanks, changing plant-tray water daily, and drying the cooler weekly. Boost immunity with vitamin C-rich fruits (amla, citrus, guava), fluids, leafy greens, oats, mung dal, and turmeric milk. Seek prompt medical care for fever, headache, retro-orbital or joint/muscle pain, or rash, with blood tests to confirm dengue or chikungunya.

articleSummary: As of 28 June 2026, UTMB researchers report a single-dose mRNA vaccine fully protects hamsters against Andes virus, a hantavirus that can spread between people via close respiratory contact. In the study, 30 vaccinated hamsters were challenged four weeks after immunization with a lethal dose; all survived with no replicating virus in tissues, while 4 of 5 unvaccinated controls died by day nine. The vaccine elicited antibodies within 14 days and protected across three dose levels (25 μg, 5 μg, 1 μg), with the lowest dose yielding antibodies in 4/5 animals. Post-exposure use is discussed, given Andes’ median human incubation of ~18 days, but remains theoretical. The work is preclinical; liver viral load was measured. NIH-supported Phase 1 trials for a one-dose regimen are planned. Notable outbreaks include Epuyén, Argentina (2018–2019; 34 cases, 11 deaths) and the May 2026 MV Hondius cruise outbreak (13 cases, 3 deaths; ~150 passengers returned to 23 countries). No Andes vaccine is approved in the Americas or Europe; inactivated hantavirus vaccines exist in China and Korea; no approved antivirals.
